title: Elements of Venezuelan Government Loyal to Chavismo Warn of Possible U.S. Assault
author: Andreína Chávez

Leaders of a key local stronghold in Caracas have been warned that the U.S. is
planning a joint operation to root out resistance and eliminate the leadership
of the 23 de Enero Parish, Juan Contreras, the main spokesperson of the Simon
Bolivar Coordinator, a 33-year-old grassroots organization, told Drop Site
News.

According to elements of the Venezuelan government loyal to Chavismo, the
political movement associated with former President Hugo Chavez, U.S. agencies
are developing plans for a "large-scale operation" targeting the well-
organized working-class stronghold, said Contreras, a prominent political
organizer and parish leader who served as a deputy in the National Assembly
between 2010 and 2015.

The State Department did not answer questions about the allegations.

23 de Enero is a densely populated, hilly parish characterized by large public
housing blocks and a thriving political life. Its proximity to Miraflores
Palace and key military posts makes it strategically important, and since 1998
it has served as an ideological stronghold for Chavismo, carrying a legacy of
popular struggle from the fall of the Perez Jimenez dictatorship in 1958
through the armed resistance movements of the 1960s-1980s against police
persecution and neoliberal policies. That legacy proved decisive during the
2002 U.S.-backed coup, when residents from the city's lower income areas
helped secure Chavez's return to power. Today, the parish is home to numerous
assembly-driven organizations, including communes that are leading the
country's socialist aspirations.

Contreras said the information reached the Coordinator "directly through an
internal source linked to patriotic officials" connected to Venezuela's
Bolivarian National Police (PNB). In a
[communique](https://www.resumenlatinoamericano.org/2026/06/04/venezuela-
grave-denuncia-de-organizaciones-chavistas-pretenden-preparar-un-operativo-
represivo-a-gran-escala-contra-la-emblematica-y-luchadora-parroquia-23-de-
enero-advierten-tambien-que-la-de/) published June 3, the Coordinator warned
of the rumored joint operation between the U.S. Drug Enforcement
Administration and the PNB's Special Tactical Operations Unit (UOTE),
operating from command centers in Flores de Catia, a sector geographically
contiguous with the 23 de Enero. Since then, according to the Simon Bolivar
Coordinator, the information has been corroborated by the group's longstanding
connections inside the Venezuelan state.

"To try to neutralize us, they intend to use rotten sectors of the police
apparatus in complicity with the DEA, attempting to impose the same infamous
narrative and framework they used to justify the act of war on January 3,"
Contreras said, warning that Washington may attempt to "falsely link social
organizations with drug trafficking and crime." Contreras said this was the
same playbook used when the U.S. branded the Nicolas Maduro government a
"cartel" to justify the abduction and transfer of the Venezuelan president and
his wife National Assembly deputy Cilia Flores to stand trial in New York on
alleged "narcoterrorism" charges. The presidential couple has pleaded not
guilty and their trial is scheduled to begin on June 1, 2027.

The DEA declined to comment.

According to Oswaldo Rivero, a popular communicator who
[reports](https://www.instagram.com/laotratvfvh/?hl=es) on the daily struggles
of working-class Venezuelans, the security forces still include officers or
sectors who hail from the country's Fourth Republic (1958-1998), when popular
leaders from the 23 de Enero parish were targeted, imprisoned, and tortured.
Rivero himself was a political prisoner in the 1980s and 1990s.

"Many of those torturers, those who persecuted us back then, remain within the
State security forces; they remain within the intelligence agencies," Rivero
told Drop Site.

In 2009, Hugo Chavez created the PBN in an effort to reform the security
forces of the Fourth Republic, including the Metropolitan Caracas Police and
the DISIP intelligence agency, which had a history of human rights abuses
involving the persecution, torture and disappearance of guerrilla, left-wing
and union activists. Many PNB commanders and officers have since been accused
of human rights violations.

The abduction of Maduro and Flores has been widely rejected by the Venezuelan
Chavista grassroots, calling for their liberation and return to Venezuela. The
U.S. justified the military strike on Venezuela on the basis that it was a
"law enforcement" operation.

"The accusations of narcoterrorism [against Maduro and Flores] are a blatant
lie that the U.S. used as an excuse to steal our oil and mineral wealth," said
Contreras, known for his long-standing popular leadership in 23 de Enero,
where he grew up and still lives.

Some in the 23 de Enero parish fear that the fight against narcotrafficking
will now be used as a smokescreen to dismantle decades of community organizing
to advance grassroots democracy, community-run production enterprises,
political formation, and self-determination within their own territories.
These self-organized community organizations now stand as one of the last
bastions of resistance to the U.S. agenda inside Venezuela.

"They want to strike the cornerstones of the Bolivarian Revolution: the
communal councils, the communes, the social movements, and historical
organizations like our Simon Bolivar Coordinator and other forces that work on
this territory," Contreras said.

**What Makes 23 de Enero a Target?**

The Simon Bolivar Coordinator has a decades-long history of armed resistance
within 23 de Enero. Founded in 1993, it united Marxist-Leninist guerrilla
groups to prioritize a more cohesive political organization mobilizing the
popular vote that eventually saw the victory of the Chavez-led Fifth Republic
Movement.

Today, the Coordinator represents one of the few remaining sources of
independent political power in a country firmly in the grasp of Washington. It
runs social programs, political education, territorial organizing and defense,
and supports communities building self-governing collectives. With the 23 de
Enero's and the Coordinator's history and proximity to power, controlling or
destabilizing the territory would directly pressure the Venezuelan government.

According to Contreras, the government of acting President Delcy Rodriguez, in
office by Constitutional mandate since January 5, is aware of the
Coordinator's public concerns about the community's safety and recently sent a
top political representative "who formally committed to thoroughly
investigating the situation."

The Rodriguez government did not respond to questions for this article.

"We understand this is also part of the cognitive warfare intended to instill
fear and demobilize," said Contreras, hinting that the U.S. may be trying to
create friction between the government and its political grassroots, which
remain an important pillar of support.

In Venezuela, the communal project and popular movement has its own ministry,
electoral processes, and leverage over political and economic decisions,
making them a likely target of U.S. action.

The Simon Bolivar Coordinator and other collectives have reinforced community
surveillance to monitor unusual police or vehicle movements at parish entry
points. Security committees from community councils and communes are holding
regular assemblies and have increased protection for communal spaces such as
radio stations, soup kitchens, cultural centers, and organizational
headquarters.

Following Maduro's removal, the Trump administration began enforcing a strict
naval blockade and operational control over Venezuela's oil exports, with the
proceeds being deposited into U.S.-controlled accounts overseen by the U.S.
Treasury Department. The Trump administration has collected more than [$13
billion](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/07/27/trump-says-us-has-sold-more-
than-13-billion-of-venezuela-oil-.html) from Venezuelan oil sales, according
to a [Financial
Times](https://www.ft.com/content/0e562e03-106e-4729-83d7-675c27eb8c4d)
estimate, but has not disclosed how that money is being used. Secretary of
State Marco Rubio told Congress in June that the money is being held in a
Citibank account and that disbursements are audited by the accounting firm
KPMG. Caracas must submit specific requests to Washington to receive
allocations of its own oil revenue, and disbursements are reportedly limited
to essential civic functions.

Washington has reiterated that a "[three-phase
process](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/rubio-says-us-plan-venezuela-is-
stability-recovery-then-transition-2026-01-07/)" of "stability, recovery, and
transition" is underway. The Rodriguez administration, balancing U.S. pressure
and a desire to survive, has begun extensive domestic and economic
reconfiguration.

Under the unequal partnership, Rodriguez has restored diplomatic ties with
Washington and carried out reforms to key legislation, such as the historical
hydrocarbon and mining laws, allowing for long-term concessions for the entry
of private and foreign capital, establishing new tax and royalty schemes, and
international dispute resolution mechanisms. The changes have undermined
Venezuelan sovereignty over its natural resources.

These overtures fall under the new cooperation agenda ushered in since January
3. But in this context, cooperation becomes a "relative term" because the
Rodriguez administration "has very little choice" in the matter, according to
Daniel DePetris, a fellow at Defense Priorities.

"Washington now effectively controls Venezuela's oil revenue and decides how,
when and where it will be allocated. Caracas simply cannot afford to ignore
Washington, let alone defy it, because doing so would jeopardize much of its
national budget and further strain an economy that is as vulnerable today as
it was when Nicolas Maduro was in power," DePetris told Drop Site.

This dynamic is ultimately one-sided, DePetris explained. "The Trump
administration will continue to use control over Venezuela's oil revenue as a
pressure tactic, both to reward the Venezuelan government when it complies
with U.S. demands and to punish it when those demands aren't met."

**U.S.-Venezuela Military Cooperation**

The newly established cooperation between the U.S. and Venezuela covers a wide
range of issues and has recently involved military and intelligence
cooperation to counter alleged drug trafficking. This makes the warnings from
23 de Enero even more urgent. On June 12, the Venezuelan government announced
that it had carried out a joint operation with the U.S. military to strike and
dismantle criminal groups operating in the mineral-rich southeastern Bolivar
state, where illegal mining has increased amid the economic crisis in recent
years.

Venezuela's Communication Ministry announced that clashes had resulted in the
death of Hector "El Niño" Guerrero, the leader of an unspecified criminal
organization, while President Donald Trump claimed on Truth Social that
Guerrero was the [leader](https://www.ice.gov/most-wanted/hector-rusthenford-
guerero-flores) of the defunct Tren de Aragua gang--a group the administration
has falsely linked to President Maduro and to migrant and drug trafficking
operations targeting the United States.

Caracas said the operation involved intelligence-sharing and technological
cooperation. The Washington Post, citing a senior U.S. administration
official, [reported](https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/2026/06/13/us-
forces-kill-venezuelan-tren-de-aragua-gang-leader-trump-says/) that the CIA
provided the intelligence leading to the strike.

Prior to the operation, General Dan Caine, the U.S. Chairman of the Joint
Chiefs of Staff, conducted a one-day visit to Caracas on June 3 while
Rodriguez was on an official trip to India. Caine met with U.S. staff and
[Marines](https://x.com/thejointstaff/status/2062277338659004865) stationed at
the U.S. Embassy in the Colinas de Valle Arriba urbanization in Caracas. The
general held bilateral discussions with [Oliver
Blanco](https://www.swissinfo.ch/spa/viceministro-venezolano-niega-militancia-
chavista-y-aboga-por-pol%C3%ADtica-exterior-%22firme%22/90986706), the
recently appointed Vice Minister for Europe and North America and a figure who
hails from the moderate opposition, on security and strengthening cooperation
mechanisms. The Venezuelan government did not issue an official statement.

Caine's visit and the joint military operation in Bolivar state confirmed the
close collaboration of U.S. intelligence and military forces with Venezuela's
security apparatus. This follows the controversial U.S. military exercise
carried out on May 23, during which two U.S. aircraft flew over the U.S.
Embassy in Caracas, and Marines disembarked in the building's parking lot.

"For the [Chavista] militant factions, seeing U.S. aircraft legally flying
over the skies of Caracas was received as a very harsh symbolic blow and a
capitulation to foreign domination," Contreras said.

Following the deadly double earthquakes that struck Caracas and La Guaira on
June 24, Washington deployed approximately 900 military personnel to La Guaira
and stationed naval vessels off Venezuela's coast, citing relief and rescue
operations as justification, according to SOUTHCOM spokesperson Steven McLoud.
The Rodriguez administration has dismissed the threat of an imminent
occupation and stated that Venezuelan authorities maintain command over the
country's emergency response and reconstruction efforts.

According to SOUTHCOM, its operations with the U.S. Air Force included
[assisting](https://x.com/Southcom/status/2081756503841841341) Venezuelan
aviation officials with air traffic control and ground operations at Simon
Bolivar International Airport, with a stated aim of clearing bottlenecks for
humanitarian aid cargo.

On July 21, as relief operations wound down, the Marine Corps' Maritime Raid
Force (MRF) [conducted
exercises](https://x.com/The24MEU/status/2079610639467561147) off the coast of
La Guaira to simulate a maritime interdiction. Since September, the U.S.
military, operating under the rubric of Operation Southern Spear, has carried
out dozens of strikes against small boats in the Caribbean Sea and Eastern
Pacific, killing at least 227 people. In a July report, the Washington Office
on Latin America [described](https://www.wola.org/analysis/killing-spree-
extrajudicial-executions-in-the-u-s-boat-strikes-campaign/) the bombings as
"murder under domestic law and extrajudicial killings under international
human rights law."

**Political Tensions**

The Rodriguez government has faced strong criticism for its compliance with
the Trump administration, the recent military cooperation and the steady
stream of U.S. officials, including CIA director John Ratcliffe, and corporate
representatives who have visited Caracas to reach energy and mining
agreements. More recently, the government has faced scrutiny over the presence
of Israeli officials, the reestablishment of diplomatic ties with Israel at a
consular level, and an AIPAC-sponsored visit of U.S. lawmakers.

In the aftermath of January 3 kidnapping of Maduro, the acting administration
forcefully condemned the U.S. for violating Venezuela's sovereignty, but has
since rapidly normalized ties with the U.S. to maintain internal political and
economic stability, while calling on the Chavista grassroots not to fall for
divisive narratives and rejecting accusations of foreign tutelage. In August,
a government delegation led by National Assembly President Jorge Rodriguez
began talks with the former opposition-majority parliament elected in 2015,
which is still recognized by the U.S. The first agreements centered around
judicial reforms and recovering 31 tons of gold withheld by the Bank of
England since 2019.

The majority of grassroots organizations, especially communes and social
movements such as Alba Movimientos, view this period as a necessary strategy:
negotiating with the erratic Trump administration to buy time for Chavismo to
regroup under more favorable conditions.

Contreras described the government's decisions as a "complex and painful
reorganization" undertaken to prevent a full-scale military escalation and to
sustain the state apparatus.

"The main contradiction today lies between the institutional leadership, which
seeks avenues for coexistence and negotiation with the occupying power, and a
grassroots community that resents the loss of sovereignty and the surrender of
strategic resources, and is seeking autonomous ways to reorganize popular
resistance," he said.
